title: To obey is better (1 Samuel 15:22)
hook: "to obey is better than sacrifice"; Saul chose the showy offering
tomorrow: The Lord looketh on the heart (1 Samuel 16:7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tall new king crouched behind the luggage at Mizpah. Your line was he hid among the baggage. What role did you stop hiding from? Today, Saul is king, and he's not hiding anymore. Day seven hundred thirty-three.

"Blessed be thou of the LORD; I have performed the commandment of the LORD." That's how Saul greets Samuel, coming back from war against Amalek. Job done, as far as he's concerned. He has even, the text mentions, set up a monument for himself on the way home, at Carmel. And Samuel stands there and asks one quiet question. What then is this bleating of sheep in my ears, and the lowing of oxen that I hear? Because Saul had been told to leave nothing of Amalek's, and here are the best of the sheep and the cattle, alive, bleating, in the background of his victory speech.
screen: `I HAVE PERFORMED THE COMMANDMENT.` → `A MONUMENT AT CARMEL.` → `WHAT IS THIS BLEATING OF SHEEP?`

segments.voice: Saul has an answer ready. The people spared the best of the sheep and oxen, he says, to sacrifice to the LORD your God. The rest we destroyed. The command he was given against Amalek is hard to read, a command to destroy everything, and this lesson won't pretend otherwise. But the chapter's own question is narrower: Saul was told one thing and did another, then dressed it up as worship. And Samuel answers. Hath the LORD as great delight in burnt-offerings and sacrifices, as in hearkening to his voice? "Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams." Listen to that pairing. To obey, and to hearken. In Hebrew, the word for obey here is the verb for hear, the same verb as in Shema, hear, O Israel. A few days ago, a boy in the sanctuary said speak, for thy servant heareth. Now a king is told that hearing is worth more than the fattest offering. Then Saul admits something. I have sinned, he says, because I feared the people, and hearkened to their voice. He did hearken. Just to the wrong voice. And even then, as Samuel turns to go, Saul asks: honor me now, I pray, before the elders of my people. Even his apology wants an audience. The prophet Hosea sounds a similar note later: God desires mercy, and not sacrifice. But here it is one king, a monument, and some bleating sheep he hoped no one would hear.
screen: `THE BEST WAS SAVED FOR SACRIFICE.` · `OBEY MEANS HEAR.` · `I FEARED THE PEOPLE.` · `HONOR ME BEFORE THE ELDERS.` · then, large: `TO OBEY IS BETTER THAN SACRIFICE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do what's asked, not what's showy. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing someone has actually asked of you lately. A partner, a parent, a boss, a friend, your own body. Not the grand gesture you'd like to make instead, the gift, the big speech, the dramatic fix. The plain thing they asked for. The dishes, the phone call, the apology without a speech. Hold it in mind, and notice whether part of you would rather do something more impressive. Then choose the plain thing. If you pray, you can hold Samuel's words: to obey is better than sacrifice. The bell holds the time.
Shema. The Hebrew verb for hear and obey, the same word Samuel used when he told Saul that obeying is worth more than the fattest offering. Today's word.
Your line: do the plain thing. Today, do one thing exactly as someone asked, plainly, with no monument and no audience. Day seven hundred thirty-three.

screen: `DAY 733 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE LORD LOOKETH ON THE HEART.`

howItsDone: Jews read Saul's war with Amalek as part of the Former Prophets, and Samuel's line that to obey is better than sacrifice is studied as a teaching about what God asks.

fork.setup: you're Samuel. Saul greets you with a blessing, says he did everything God asked, and you can hear sheep that shouldn't be there. what do you do?
options: ask him about the bleating of the sheep.
offer the sheep as a sacrifice yourself.
fork.reveal: Samuel asks one question: what then is this bleating of sheep in my ears? the showy offering falls apart, and the answer is: to obey is better than sacrifice.

original.note: Hebrew: to hear, the word translated 'to obey' in 1 Samuel 15:22.

trapdoor: what you thought: do as you're told.
what it means: a king told to do one thing does another, calls it worship, and is told that hearing God matters more than the grandest offering.
what a scholar hears: the Hebrew for 'to obey' is shemoa, to hear, the verb of the Shema. Saul hearkened, just to the people.

notes: Audit: 'here it starts' (an implied first) changed to 'here it is'.
Verify JPS 1917 wording of 15:13 and 15:22 (certain in the KJV; the KJV has a colon in 15:13).
The herem command against Amalek (15:3) is acknowledged as hard and not explained or defended; a Keeper should decide whether a fuller note (e.g., rabbinic readings) belongs on this day.
Shemoa (15:22) as the verb shama, 'hear', the verb of Deuteronomy 6:4: a grammatical fact, but under the strict claims rule a Keeper should confirm it may stay.
'The prophets after Samuel come back to this theme again and again' is softened to 'later prophets return to this theme' (cf. Hosea 6:6, Amos 5:21–24, Isaiah 1:11–17); a Keeper may soften or cut it.
15:14, 15:24 and 15:30 are paraphrased close to the text without quotation marks.
